meta.title: Media Literacy and Critical Discourse Analysis
meta.targetAudience: Intermediate Middle School ESL Students (CEFR B1 Level)

weeks.title: Media Impact & Narrative Sovereignty
weeks.summary: Students learn to check online source reliability, identify domain suffixes, evaluate author credibility, and complete a Fact-Checker Matrix.

logistics.layout: Collaborative desk pods of 4 students to support peer evaluation.

phases.title: Hook & Priming
phases.facilitatorActions: Ask students where they discover news online. Project 'How do we know if a story is real or fake?' on the screen.
phases.script: Welcome team! Today we start our journey as Media Detectives. Look at this headline on the screen. Do you believe it immediately, or do you ask questions first?

phases.title: Guided Source Analysis
phases.facilitatorActions: Introduce domain suffixes (.go.id, .com, .blogspot.com) and demonstrate author verification using Sample Card #1.
phases.script: Notice the domain URL. A government or official educational domain like .go.id carries higher trust than an anonymous blog post.

phases.title: Group Work & Fact-Checking Matrix
phases.facilitatorActions: Distribute Website Sample Cards #2-#4. Have student pods analyze author credentials, evidence, and assign trust scores.
phases.script: Work with your pod. Use the mandatory sentence frame to justify whether each card receives a Green, Yellow, or Red trust score.

phases.title: Wrap-Up & Reflection
phases.facilitatorActions: Review answers using the Week 1 Answer Key and debrief key indicators of fake news.
phases.script: Who can tell me why Card #2 received a Red rating despite having an exciting headline?

slides.title: VOICES OF RIAU: International Youth Journalism & Cultural Advocacy
slides.content:
# SESSION 1: SECONDARY EDUCATION (GRADES 7-10 / CEFR B1-C1)

Welcome to the active international newsroom. Over the next unit, you are not just practicing English—you are working as investigative reporters, editors, and producers reclaiming the narrative of our home region.
slides.speakerNotes: Welcome team. Today, our classroom officially transforms into an active international newsroom. Over the next seven weeks, you are not just practicing English—you are working as investigative reporters, editors, and producers reclaiming the narrative of our home region.

slides.title: The Headline Challenge: Media Impact
slides.content:
### Comparing Media Framing

* **Headline A (External Deficit Framing)**: *"Disaster in Sumatra: Fragile Peatlands Face Irreversible Destruction."*
  * **Emotional Impact**: Creates a sense of total tragedy and helplessness.
  * **Agency**: Portrays local residents as passive, helpless victims.

* **Headline B (Solution & Agency Framing)**: *"Riau Communities Deploy Local Hydrology Systems to Restore Historic Peatland Ecosystems."*
  * **Emotional Impact**: Inspires purpose and systemic problem-solving.
  * **Agency**: Highlights local specialists actively restoring land stewardship.
slides.speakerNotes: Examine the two headlines. Notice how word choice and framing completely change how the reader perceives the community's power and actions.

slides.title: Core Concept: Narrative Sovereignty
slides.content:
### Definition
The right and power of a community to tell their own stories, represent their own culture, and control how their reality is reported globally.

* **Story Ownership**: Local youth replace external news crews with authentic, primary-source investigation.
* **Global Reach**: Utilizing precise international English (CEFR B1-C1) to broadcast Riau's true context to world audiences.
slides.speakerNotes: Narrative sovereignty means taking control of our own representation instead of relying on external media crews.

slides.title: Reporting Styles: Deficit vs. Agency
slides.content:
### Deficit-Based Framing (AVOID)
Focuses exclusively on problems, poverty, damage, or helplessness in a region while ignoring local leadership.
> *"A deficit implies something is lacking. It portrays communities strictly by what they lack rather than what they build."*

---

### Agency-Based Reporting (OUR GOAL)
Investigates real ecological challenges while documenting community land stewardship, local hydrologists, and solutions.
> *"Agency focuses on the capacity of local leaders and youth to act independently and solve complex problems."*
slides.speakerNotes: Always challenge deficit framing. As newsroom reporters, your goal is to highlight community action and agency.

slides.title: Case Study: Kampar Peatlands - Beyond the Disaster Script
slides.content:
* **The Deficit Script**: For decades, global crews arrived during dry seasons to capture haze footage, labeling Riau an 'environmental catastrophe zone.'
* **Restoring the Full Picture**: Local hydrologists, village fire-prevention teams (*Masyarakat Peduli Api*), and youth activists actively manage and restore these vital peatlands.
* **Reporters' Duty**: Investigate both the challenges and the engineered solutions.
slides.speakerNotes: Look beyond the disaster script. Ensure your reports include local hydrologists and fire-prevention teams actively managing the peatlands.

slides.title: The Three Pillars of Newsroom Ethics
slides.content:
1. **Accuracy & Verification**: Never publish a claim without at least two primary source verifications and direct evidence from field research.
2. **Informed Consent**: Interview subjects must know WHO you are, WHERE the story goes, and explicitly AGREE to be recorded.
3. **Balance & Context**: Avoid sensational tragedy. Always include local agency, background history, and systemic context.
slides.speakerNotes: Every international journalist operates under strict ethics. These three pillars keep our newsroom professional and trusted.

slides.title: The 4-Step Ethical Interview Checklist
slides.content:
* **1. Clear Identification**: Introduce yourself by name, school, and your role with the VOICES OF RIAU youth newsroom.
* **2. Project Transparency**: Explain clearly what the story is about and where it will be published (podcast or digital web journal).
* **3. Informed Consent**: Ask explicitly: *"Do I have your permission to record our conversation and use your name in our report?"*
* **4. Right to Pause**: Inform the subject: *"You can pause the interview or decline to answer any question at any time."*
slides.speakerNotes: Review this 4-step checklist with your newsroom pod before conducting any audio or video interviews.

slides.title: Selecting Your Newsroom Beat
slides.content:
* **Desk 1: Ecology & Conservation**: Rainforest biodiversity, peatland hydrology, wildlife corridor protection, and community forestry programs.
* **Desk 2: Energy & Economics**: Renewable energy transitions, sustainable palm oil practices, carbon markets, and regional green economics.
* **Desk 3: Youth Culture & Identity**: Civic activism, indigenous Malay and Sea Tribe heritage preservation, and digital youth expression.
slides.speakerNotes: Choose your newsroom beat carefully. Each desk focuses on critical regional issues requiring deep investigation.

slides.title: Media Framing & Perspective Matrix
slides.content:
| Analysis Metric | External / Global Report | Local / Solution-Oriented Report |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Headline & Tone** | *"Catastrophe Strikes Peatlands"* | *"Villagers Deploy Canal Blocks"* |
| **Primary Focus** | Uncontrolled destruction & damage | Active restoration & hydrological engineering |
| **Featured Sources** | Outside NGO directors, foreign commentators | Local hydrologists, community leaders, youth |
| **Portrayal of Residents** | Helpless bystanders, passive victims | Active problem-solvers & land stewards |
slides.speakerNotes: Compare these metrics. Use this table when auditing external media sources.

slides.title: Exit Ticket: Rewriting for Agency
slides.content:
### Original Biased Excerpt
> *"Remote villages in Riau remain trapped in economic hardship as traditional palm oil methods face mounting international criticism."*
* **Issue**: Uses loaded deficit terms (*"trapped"*, *"hardship"*) and ignores local agricultural innovation.

### Journalistic Rewrite Criteria
* Use active, objective register.
* Restore community action and specific context.
* Highlight transition to sustainable farming standards.
slides.speakerNotes: Complete your exit ticket by rewriting the biased excerpt to reflect agency, action, and sustainable progress.

weeks.title: Word Choice, Tone & Headline Manipulation
weeks.summary: Students analyze lexical bias, exaggerated clickbait language, and practice rewriting sensational headlines into neutral, factual statements.

logistics.layout: Desk pods with side-by-side comparative text stations.

phases.title: Hook & Priming
phases.facilitatorActions: Project contrasting headlines: 'Local Park Reopens After Repairs' vs. 'SHOCKING DISASTER AT LOCAL PARK'.
phases.script: Look at these two headlines describing the exact same event. How does the emotional language in the second headline alter your feelings?

phases.title: Lexical Bias & Tone Analysis
phases.facilitatorActions: Teach students to spot loaded adjectives, emotional clickbait, and sensationalized verbs.
phases.script: Words like 'SHOCKING', 'MIRACLE', or 'MUST SEE' trigger emotional reactions rather than informing you with facts.

phases.title: Headline Transformation Exercise
phases.facilitatorActions: Students identify clickbait triggers on TikTok/WhatsApp cards and rewrite them into factual news statements.
phases.script: Strip away the emotional noise. Rebuild the headline using clear, neutral vocabulary.

phases.title: Peer Review & Debrief
phases.facilitatorActions: Have students present their neutral rewrites to their pod.
phases.script: Compare your neutral rewrite with your neighbor's. Did you both remove the emotional bias effectively?

weeks.title: Spotting Opinion vs. Fact & Ads
weeks.summary: Students categorize media into Objective Fact, Editorial Opinion, and Native Advertising using key indicator vocabulary and contrast connectors.

logistics.layout: Collaborative desk pods with sorting stations for media portfolio cards.

phases.title: Hook & Priming
phases.facilitatorActions: Project three contrasting snippets: an objective report, an opinion piece, and a sponsored article.
phases.script: Can you tell which of these articles is trying to inform you, which is giving an opinion, and which is secretly trying to sell you a product?

phases.title: Media Categorization & Key Indicators
phases.facilitatorActions: Teach indicator terms (e.g., 'data proves', 'in my view', 'sponsored content', 'promoted').
phases.script: Notice words like 'I believe' or 'should' indicate opinion, whereas metrics and official data signal objective facts.

phases.title: Portfolio Sorting Activity
phases.facilitatorActions: Groups analyze Media Sample Cards #1-#4 and complete their categorization worksheet using contrast connectors.
phases.script: Use contrast connectors like 'however', 'on the other hand', and 'unlike' when justifying your classifications.

phases.title: Review & Class Discussion
phases.facilitatorActions: Review sorted cards using the Week 3 Answer Key.
phases.script: Why is Card #3 considered an advertisement despite looking like a regular beauty blog post?

weeks.title: Comparing Two Sides of a Story
weeks.summary: Students conduct side-by-side comparative analysis of paired news articles covering the same event to evaluate emphasis, framing, and omissions.

logistics.layout: Desk pods equipped with side-by-side comparative analysis stations.

phases.title: Hook & Priming
phases.facilitatorActions: Project contrasting headlines: 'New City LRT Brings 500 Jobs' vs. 'LRT Construction Forces Shophouse Closures'.
phases.script: Both articles discuss the new LRT train line. Why does one feel like great news while the other feels like a community disaster?

phases.title: Comparative Analysis Framework
phases.facilitatorActions: Demonstrate how to analyze focus, main ideas, included details, and omitted perspectives using Pair #1.
phases.script: When an article omits specific facts, it creates a selective bias. Look at what is missing just as closely as what is written.

phases.title: Group Side-by-Side Matrix Work
phases.facilitatorActions: Pods complete the Side-by-Side Comparison Matrix for Article Pair #2 (Digital Textbooks vs. Screen Time Overload).
phases.script: Fill out your comparative matrices using the mandatory comparative sentence frames.

phases.title: Class Synthesis & Debate
phases.facilitatorActions: Facilitate group presentation of comparison findings.
phases.script: Which article provided a more balanced perspective, and what critical details were omitted?

weeks.title: Group Project: The Media Investigation
weeks.summary: Student teams operate as editorial newsroom pods to investigate assigned media dossiers and build a structured 4-slide media audit presentation.

logistics.layout: Collaborative newsroom pods equipped with shared digital presentation templates.

phases.title: Editorial Briefing & Setup
phases.facilitatorActions: Assign newsroom pods and distribute Media Case Dossiers (SuperEnergy Drink, Health Notice, AI Teachers, Eco Project).
phases.script: Welcome newsroom teams. Today you begin your group investigation. Your goal is to audit your assigned media item and prepare a 4-slide report.

phases.title: Group Investigation & Analysis
phases.facilitatorActions: Guide pods through examining author intent, target audience, bias indicators, and missing evidence.
phases.script: Assign specific speaking roles for each slide. Ensure every speaker uses mandatory academic signposting phrases.

phases.title: Slide Deck Construction
phases.facilitatorActions: Assist students in completing their 4-Slide Planning Worksheets and digital slide drafts.
phases.script: Slide 1 introduces your source, Slide 2 details word choice, Slide 3 exposes bias or omission, and Slide 4 delivers your final verdict.

phases.title: Progress Check & Facilitator Feedback
phases.facilitatorActions: Review draft plans and provide formative feedback before Week 6 presentations.
phases.script: Rehearse your presentation transition frames before our final showcase next week.

worksheet.title: 4-Slide Investigation Planning Worksheet
worksheet.instructions: Plan your group's 4-slide presentation script. Assign speaking roles and mandatory signposting frames for each slide.

defaultRows.signpostingFrame: First, we examined [Source Title], created by [Author/Publisher] on [Date].
Moving to language analysis, we noticed loaded words such as '[Word]' which create a [Tone] tone.
On the other hand, the author completely omits any mention of [Omitted Detail].
In conclusion, based on our investigation, we rate this source as [Green / Yellow / Red] because...

weeks.title: The Media Literacy Showcase & Review
weeks.summary: Student newsrooms deliver 4-slide media audit presentations, engage in polite peer questioning, and complete program self-reflections.

logistics.layout: Conference presentation stage setup with audience seating facing the podium.

phases.title: Showcase Briefing & Setup
phases.facilitatorActions: Brief the class on audience protocol, scoring rubrics, and polite peer questioning rules.
phases.script: Welcome to the Media Literacy Showcase! As audience members, your job is to listen critically and ask respectful questions using our reference frames.

phases.title: Group Presentations & Q&A
phases.facilitatorActions: Newsroom pods present their 4-slide media audits. Peer groups ask follow-up questions.
phases.script: Thank you Team 1. We now open the floor for one polite question from the audience.

phases.title: Comprehensive Program Review
phases.facilitatorActions: Synthesize key learnings from across all 6 weeks (URLs, tone, fact vs. opinion, comparative framing).
phases.script: Reflect on how far you have come—from accepting headlines at face value to analyzing critical discourse like expert journalists.

phases.title: Self-Reflection & Graduation
phases.facilitatorActions: Students complete their individual self-reflection forms and celebrate unit completion.
phases.script: Congratulations Media Detectives! Carry these analytical tools with you whenever you read news online.

worksheet.title: Student Self-Reflection & Evaluation Sheet
worksheet.instructions: Reflect on your growth as a critical media reader over the past 6 weeks.

fields.label: What is the most important skill you learned?
How will you read social media or news differently now?
Which week's activity was most engaging and why?
